column1: # The four source corpora leave 52 of the installation's 288 seed lineages
# stalled one or two steps below the surface: "token" stops dead at Middle
# English, "code" at French, "abyss" nowhere at all. The gaps are not errors in
# the etymology, they are gaps in what got scraped in 2018.
# The 2018 README set out to "find new connections that were not already
# present in current taxonomy". This file is that, done with an LLM instead of
# a character-level LSTM: each row is a link absent from all four corpora,
# proposed with a gloss. They are standard scholarly etymologies, not
# inventions — but because no source corpus asserts them, the installation
# draws them in their own register (pulsing, ringed) rather than passing them
# off as attested. See dreams.tsv for the inventions.
# child <TAB> rel:conjecture <TAB> parent <TAB> gloss of the parent <TAB> confidence
# confidence: high   = uncontroversial, in any standard reference
#             medium = generally accepted, some disagreement on the details
#             low    = one plausible account among several

column4: to lay in a surrounding mass
a garden plot; a sleeping place
a linen thread; a drawn line
to carry in, to bring forward
law, custom, that which is allotted
a sign, a mark, a grave-marker

column1: # Every word in this movement descends from *teks-, "to weave". The corpus knew

column4: fine, thin — literally under the warp
a web, a warp on the loom
to weave in front of, to fringe
to rub, to twist, to bore
a line, a cord, a sinew
an unformed mass; the unfinished thing in Psalm 139
gift of god — the pet name became the toy

column1: # The corpus had "glamour" descending from Scots gramarye and stopped, missing
# that gramarye is "grammar": literacy was indistinguishable from sorcery.

column4: to speak, to plead, to pray
to laugh, to smile, to be astonished

column1: # "noise" descends, through Old French, from Latin nausea — seasickness — and
# so from naus, a ship. In a piece projected as an ocean this is not decoration.

column4: a cut, a division — the land's cut edge
a tree; and trust, truth, troth
a birth, a breed, a people

column1: # "code" was a tree trunk; "pattern" was a father; "cipher" and "zero" are the
# same Arabic word for emptiness, arriving by two different routes.

column4: a tree trunk; a block of wood split into tablets
a protector, a model to be copied
a tally, two halves thrown together to prove identity

column1: # "oku" — to read — is Old Turkic oqı-, to call out: reading was reciting aloud.
# "örgü" (knitting) and "örümcek" (spider) are the same verb ör-, to weave.

column4: to call, to summon, to recite aloud
to plait, to weave, to braid
to fall; and so, to occur to one
reason — from the root meaning to tie, to bind fast
a phantom, an apparition, an image
to be able, to have power

column1: # "divan" is the deepest chain in the piece. The sofa you sit on is named for a
# Persian account-book, which is named for an Old Persian word for writing,
# which is a Sumerian clay tablet.

column4: an archive, a collection of written sheets
tea, in the Amoy dialect the Dutch traded through
a raised bench, a stone ledge
a carob seed, used as a jeweller's weight
a little horn; a carob seed
to set a bone, to restore
the fine powder of antimony used to darken the eyes
a turban — the flower was named for the shape
a dry powder for treating wounds
lapis lazuli; the place it was mined
a buffoon, a thing of ridicule
a piece, a fragment of sugar
king — the game is named for the warning "the king"
of the Seres, the silk people
to wrap up, to fold together
to bind fast, and so to be able to reason
a notification, an inventory of fees

column1: # ---- Semitic and Iranian roots as their own era ------------------------------
# Arabic is tagged as a living language, so a triconsonantal root reached from
# English sat on the surface and these lineages never descended. Classical
# Arabic (arb) and Biblical Hebrew (hbo) give the root stage its own era, the
# way Latin does for French and Middle Persian does for Persian.

column4: the root: to be empty, to whistle in a bare place
jasmine — Persian, a gift of God
the root: to range in a row, to line up
the root: to darken the rim of the eye
the root: to dwell, to be resident
the root: to seem, to appear as a horseman in the dark
the root: to tie a camel's foreleg, and so to reason
the root: to wrap, to fold shut over
the root: to wrap, to fold shut over
the root: to make, to fabricate
tea, in the dialect the Dutch traded through

column1: # The single largest gap in the 2018 data: 33,145 English words stall at Old or
# Middle English and never reach Proto-Germanic, let alone Proto-Indo-European.
# It is not a gap in scholarship -- every one of these is in any standard
# reference -- it is the Etymonline scrape truncating the most common words in
# all stopped dead one step above their real ancestry.
# This fills the commonest of them, ordered by how connected the word is, so a
# visitor searching for an ordinary English word gets a real dive instead of
# ---- the ones that had no Old English step recorded at all -----------------

column4: man-age: the span of a human life, and so the earth
silver — a loan into Germanic from an unknown source
a bit, a morsel; later, bread
that which is broken or leavened
hair of a tail, a tail
a boy, a youth, a servant
the inside of the mouth, palate

column1: # ---- the ones that reached Old English and stopped there -------------------

column4: moon, and therefore month, the thing measured
to care for, to desire, to love
to be weak, to go slack
a circle, a wheel — a reduplication of "to turn"
a worker in metal or wood
to defecate — to separate from oneself
of obscure origin; attested only in English
to lie down, to settle, to be dear
the ground, the soil, the world
the ground, the soil, the world
to go, to transport in a vehicle

column1: # ---- the commonest Latin and French arrivals that also stalled ------------

column4: the mint — from the temple of Juno Moneta, where Rome struck coin
a plank, a board, a writing tablet
to take, to accept, and so to teach
a stake, a gallows, a cross
a mark, a sign, a written note
a boundary, a sign, a limit
the boxwood tree, and vessels turned from it
Cyprian metal — the island was Rome's source
to mark out, to tread a boundary

column1: # ---- surface forms that never recorded their Old English step -------------
# The chain above each of these existed already; what was missing was the first
# hop, so the modern word could not reach it.

column4: to care for, to desire, to love
fire, considered as a substance rather than a living force
a dwelling, an estate, a village
tree, wood, and also truth and trust
winter, and so a year of one's age
